label: M3 S2 | The F4 Toggle & Reference Behaviour

before.body: You do not need to manually type $ signs. Click on a cell reference inside a formula and press F4 to cycle through all four referencing modes.
before.mac_note: On Mac, F4 may require pressing Fn + F4 if your function keys are mapped to system controls. Alternatively, use ⌘ + T in some Excel for Mac versions.

shortcuts.action: Enter formula and stay in cell

worked_example.setup: Cell B1 contains Reliance Industries' FY24 revenue: ₹2,59,000 Cr. Cell C1 contains the growth assumption: 12%. Project revenue for FY25–FY28 in cells B2 through B5.

results.explanation: B1 is relative (points to row above), $C$1 is locked
B2 is relative (now points to B2), $C$1 still locked

worked_example.sensitivity_warning: If you had used a relative reference (C1 without $ signs) and copied the formula down, B3 would reference C2 (which is empty or wrong), B4 would reference C3, and so on. The model silently breaks — no error message, just wrong numbers.

after.body: You do not need to manually type $ signs. Click on a cell reference inside a formula and press F4 to cycle through all four referencing modes.

f4_cycle.plain_english: Both row and column are fixed. When you copy this formula anywhere on the sheet, the reference always points to cell A1. Use this when a cell contains a constant (like a tax rate or exchange rate) that should never change during copying.

The row stays fixed at 1, but the column adjusts when copied left or right. Row always points to row 1, but the column letter changes. Useful when copying a formula horizontally across a single data row that contains reference values.

The column stays fixed at A, but the row adjusts when copied up or down. Column always points to column A, but the row number changes. Useful when copying a formula vertically down a single reference column.

Both row and column shift as you copy. When copied down one row, A1 becomes A2; when copied right one column, A1 becomes B1. This is the default mode and is used for most calculations where you want the reference to move with the formula.

after.mac_note: On Mac, F4 may require pressing Fn + F4 if your function keys are mapped to system controls. Alternatively, use ⌘ + T in some Excel for Mac versions.

shortcuts.action: Enter formula and stay in cell

worked_example.setup: Cell B1 contains Reliance Industries' FY24 revenue: ₹2,59,000 Cr. Cell C1 contains the growth assumption: 12%. Project revenue for FY25–FY28 in cells B2 through B5.

variables.meaning: Prior year revenue (relative reference — updates as formula copies down)
Growth rate assumption (absolute reference — always locks to C1)

worked_example.plain_english: This formula takes the prior year's revenue and multiplies it by (1 + growth rate) to project the next year. The $ signs around C1 ensure the growth rate stays constant while B1 adjusts row-by-row as you copy down. Without the $ signs, the growth reference would shift to C2, C3, and so on—silently breaking your model.
computation: Step 1: Identify the reference that should never change (C1, the growth rate) and lock it with $ signs: $C$1
Step 2: Leave the data reference (B1) relative so it adjusts automatically when copied down to B2, B3, etc.
Step 3: Enter =B1*(1+$C$1) in cell B2 and press Ctrl+Enter (or ⌘+Enter on Mac)
Step 4: Select B2, then press Ctrl+D (or ⌘+D on Mac) to fill down through B5; the relative reference updates, the absolute reference stays locked

results.explanation: B1 is relative (points to row above), $C$1 is locked
B2 is relative (now points to B2), $C$1 still locked

worked_example.sensitivity_warning: If you had used a relative reference (C1 without $ signs) and copied the formula down, B3 would reference C2 (which is empty or wrong), B4 would reference C3, and so on. The model silently breaks — no error message, just wrong numbers.
worked_example.insight: The F4 toggle saves you from the most common copy-paste error in financial models: forgetting to lock a constant reference. In India equity research, models often reference a single tax rate, inflation assumption, or exchange rate across hundreds of rows. F4 ensures those locks are in place without manual typing of $ signs.
